name: Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts
title: Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts
answer: Yield strategies in smart contracts are on-chain programs that allocate crypto assets to earn a return, typically through lending, liquidity provision, staking, or a combination of these. They sit within decentralised finance and cover both simple single-protocol deposits and multi-step strategies that move funds between venues. The scope includes the design of the strategy, the contracts that execute it, and the tokens or claims that represent a user's share. It does not include off-chain yield products that merely use a blockchain for settlement.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Yield strategies in smart contracts are on-chain programs that allocate crypto assets to earn a return, typically through lending, liquidity provision, staking, or a combination of these. They sit within decentralised finance and cover both simple single-protocol deposits and multi-step strategies that move funds between venues. The scope includes the design of the strategy, the contracts that execute it, and the tokens or claims that represent a user's share. It does not include off-chain yield products that merely use a blockchain for settlement.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These strategies run on public blockchains, most often Ethereum or other networks compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine. They depend on non-custodial wallets for user control, nodes and remote procedure call providers for reading and writing state, and price oracles for valuation and liquidation triggers. Bridges and layer two networks extend the reach of a strategy across chains, while block explorers and indexers provide the data needed to monitor positions. Gas fees and block times shape what is economically viable on each network.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by smart contracts that hold user deposits and follow coded rules to supply assets to lending markets, provide liquidity to automated market makers, or stake tokens in validation or restaking protocols. Many strategies compound rewards automatically, rebalance collateral, or rotate between venues when yields change. Keepers and bots execute time-sensitive actions such as liquidations or harvests, often in exchange for a fee. The yield itself comes from borrower interest, trading fees, token emissions, or a mix of these sources.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in these strategies turn on the provenance of the contracts and the powers retained by their authors. Users typically hold a claim on the pool or vault, not on the underlying assets directly, and that claim is enforced by code and sometimes by a governance token. Risks include smart contract bugs, oracle manipulation, impermanent loss, liquidation cascades, and admin keys that can upgrade or pause a contract. Provenance matters, so audits, open source code, timelocks, and multisig controls are common signals of how much trust a strategy requires. Regulatory treatment varies by jurisdiction and can affect who may use a strategy and how returns are taxed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more automated and cross-chain strategies, with AI agents increasingly used to monitor conditions and adjust allocations. Tokenised real-world assets and regulated yield products are bringing traditional collateral on chain, which changes the risk and compliance profile of many strategies. Institutional participation is growing, but so is scrutiny from regulators over whether certain yield offerings are securities. Expect continued experimentation with restaking, liquid staking, and intent-based architectures, alongside a push for better risk disclosure and standardised audits.
